title: Ashtpadi 20, salok: wandering, I came
hook: phirat phirat: wandering and wandering, I have come to Your refuge (Sukhmani 20)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 19, and your line: live light. Did the give pile from the drawer find a new home? Today a new ashtpadi begins, the twentieth, with a traveler who finally stops. Day five hundred fourteen.

Phirat phirat. Say it out loud and it sounds like footsteps: phirat, phirat, phirat. It's the first word of the twentieth ashtpadi, and it means wandering, turning, going round and round. A car circles a city at night, looking for an address. Left, then left again, back past the same gas station, the phone saying recalculating. And then, finally, the right door, the porch light on, and someone saying come in. Today's salok is that moment of arrival.
screen: `PHIRAT, PHIRAT: LIKE FOOTSTEPS.` → `RECALCULATING.` → `THE PORCH LIGHT ON.`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines. In paraphrase: wandering and wandering, O God, I have come, and fallen at Your sanctuary. This is Nanak's prayer, O God: attach me to Your devotion. Start with the repeated word. Gurbani often doubles a word to make it last: phirat phirat isn't one detour, it's a whole life of them. Some readers hear in it the long round of births and deaths, the soul turning through lifetime after lifetime. Others hear the ordinary wandering of a single life: job to job, want to want, one more thing that was supposed to finally make it feel settled. The text holds both. Then the verb: I have come, aaiaa. Not I have earned my way in, or I have found the answer. Just: I'm here. And then pariaa: I've fallen, or I've laid myself down, at Your saran, Your refuge. It's the posture of someone too tired to keep standing. The last line is the request. Notice what it doesn't ask for. It doesn't ask for the wandering to have been worth it, or for a prize at the end. It asks: attach me to Your bhagti, Your devotion. Keep me here. After nineteen ashtpadis of teaching, of lists and pictures and warnings, the twentieth opens with no argument at all. Just a traveler at the door, and a request to stay.
screen: `THE SALOK: I HAVE COME, I HAVE FALLEN.` · `PHIRAT PHIRAT: A WHOLE LIFE OF DETOURS.` · `NOT EARNED, JUST ARRIVED.` · `THE REQUEST: KEEP ME HERE.` · then, large: `I HAVE COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop and rest. Wherever you are, let yourself arrive. Feel the weight of your body settle into the chair or the floor, as if you'd just walked a long way. Let the shoulders drop. With each breath out, you can silently say: I have come. Nothing to fix for two minutes, nowhere else to get to. If thoughts start wandering, notice the footsteps, phirat phirat, and come back. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 20. Its salok: after long wandering, phirat phirat, the seeker arrives at God's refuge and asks only to be kept in devotion.
Your line: I have come. Today, the next time you walk through a door, your own or anyone's, pause on the threshold for one breath and arrive. Day five hundred fourteen.

screen: `DAY 514 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A BEGGAR AT THE DOOR.`

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twentieth ashtpadi begin with its salok, in which the seeker, after long wandering, comes to God's refuge and asks only to be joined to devotion.

pairs: devotion, what the salok asks for

myth: the salok ends by asking for a reward for the long journey
it asks only to be attached to God's devotion.
Gurbani often doubles a word to make it last
phirat phirat: not one detour, a whole life of them.
the salok says the seeker earned the way in
the seeker simply comes, and falls at the refuge.

fork.setup: after a long wandering, you reach the door. what does the twentieth salok ask for?
options: proof that the wandering was worth it.
to be attached to devotion, and kept here.
fork.reveal: Nanak's prayer in the salok is simply: attach me to Your devotion. no argument, no prize, just a request to stay.

original.note: Gurmukhi: phirat, wandering, going round; doubled in the salok as phirat phirat.

trapdoor: what you thought: wandering, I came is about getting lost on a trip.
what it means: a whole life of turning, ending at God's refuge with one request: keep me in devotion.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear in phirat phirat the long round of births and deaths, the soul turning through many lives before it reaches the refuge.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 20, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 289)

notes: Paraphrase of the ashtpadi 20 salok (phirat phirat prabh aaiaa pariaa tau sarnaai; nanak kee prabh bentee apnee bhagtee laai): confirm wording and Ang 289.
The reading of phirat phirat as the round of births is offered as one way many Sikhs hear it; a Keeper may refine.
Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer uses the 'anyone who has... knows the feeling' opener (day 510 used the same one); 'many Sikhs hear' softened to 'some readers'.
